name: ETag and HTTP cache supercookie
plain: A tracker stores an ID in the cache validators of a file, which come back on every request.
meaning: A server sets a unique ETag or Last-Modified on a resource; the browser sends If-None-Match back, identifying the visitor. Since cache partitioning (Chrome 86, Firefox 85, Safari earlier) the ID is only valid per top-level site.

steps: Later request sends If-None-Match with the ID

limits.headline: Can try to tag your browser with a hidden cached ID, though browsers now limit it
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when you visit a site that tries it
can: Store an ID in the cache details of a file
Recognise a returning visitor on the same site
Keep the ID after you clear cookies in older browsers
cannot: Follow you across different sites; modern browsers separate the cache by site
Survive clearing your cache or browsing data
Work the same in every browser
limits.differs: Chrome, Firefox and Safari all split the cache by site now, so the ID only works inside one site.

story.what_it_is: A tracker hides a personal ID in a saved file's label, so it survives clearing cookies.

marketing.name: HTTP cache partitioning
marketing.pitch: Chrome describes splitting the cache by site so one site cannot learn about your visits to another through shared cached files.

story.for_you: You never see it. You clear your cookies and still get recognized, because the ID rides on a cached file. Modern browsers now keep separate caches per site, which weakens this trick.
story.for_makers: Trackers and ad firms used it as a backup when cookies were blocked or deleted. It is mostly unfriendly to privacy, and browsers have been closing it with split caches.

use_cases.example: An ad network labels a tiny image with a unique tag and reads it back to recognize you on the next visit.
An analytics script rebuilds a lost ID from the cache label after cookies are cleared.
A fraud company uses it to link a returning bot or a banned account.
A retargeting service recognizes a shopper who deleted cookies and shows the same product ads.
A game portal links a banned player's new browser session to the old one.
A video site recognizes a viewer who tried to dodge a free article limit.

technical_bounds: Cross-site ID no longer works; same-site ID still works
